{{short description|American solar physicist}}
'''Carol Jo Crannell''' (November 15, 1938 – May 10, 2009) was a [[solar physics|solar physicist]] known for her work on [[solar flare]]s and on the astrophysical observation of [[x-ray]]s and [[gamma ray]]s. She worked for thirty years at the [[NASA]] [[Goddard Space Flight Center]].{{r|wapo|engle}}

==Life==
Crannell was born in [[Columbus, Ohio]].
She graduated from [[Miami University]] in 1960, and completed her Ph.D. in physics at [[Stanford University]] in 1967, with [[Robert Hofstadter]] as her [[doctoral advisor]].{{r|engle}} She worked at the Goddard Space Flight Center from 1974 until 2004, when she retired.{{r|wapo|engle}}

Crannell also held an adjunct faculty position at [[Catholic University of America]],{{r|wapo}} where her husband, Hall L. Crannell, is an emeritus professor.{{r|cua}} Her daughter, [[Annalisa Crannell]], is a mathematician at [[Franklin & Marshall College]].{{r|grandma}}

==Research==
Crannell's doctoral research concerned [[particle shower]]s.
At Goddard, Crannell pushed for x-ray and gamma-ray observations of the sun, and led balloon-mounted experiments to make these observations.{{r|engle}}

==Activism==
Crannell played an active role in the struggle for equal opportunity for women in physics. She chaired the Committee on the Status of Women in Physics of the American Physical Society, and helped found the ''CSWP Gazette'', the newsletter of the Committee. Through her position at the Catholic University she also helped bring underrepresented students to summer internships at Goddard.{{r|engle}}

==Recognition==
Crannell became a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1992, and a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1998. In 1990, Women in Aerospace gave her their Outstanding Achievement Award "for her dedication to expanding women’s opportunities for career advancement and for increasing their visibility through her activities as an aerospace professional".{{r|engle}}
